title: Polynomial-time private release of all marginals
formal: Do there exist an integer \(C\ge 1, a\) function \(\alpha :N_{\ge 2}\to [0,1]\) with \(\lim _{d\to \infty}\alpha (d)=0, a\) uniform randomized mechanism M and a uniform deterministic evaluator E, such that for every \(d\ge 2\) and every database \(D\in (\{0,1\}^{d})^{n}\) with \(n=d^{C}, M\) runs in time polynomial in n,d, satisfies \((1,1/(100n^{2}))\)-differential privacy under replacement of one row, and outputs a finite synopsis S for which, with probability at least \(2/3, E(S,q)\) approximates \(q(D)\) within \(\alpha (d)\) simultaneously for every marginal query q?
definitions: A marginal query is a pair \((J,a)\), where \(J\subseteq \{1,\ldots ,d\}\) and \(a\in \{0,1\}^{J}\), and \(q_{J,a}(D)=|\){\(i\in \{1,\ldots ,n\}:D_{ij}=a_{j}\) for all \(j\in J\)}|/n. The empty J query has value one. Queries of every order up to d are included. The database is an explicitly stored ordered n-by-d bit matrix; neighbouring databases have the same dimensions and differ in exactly one row. Differential privacy means that for every ordered pair of neighbours \(D,D'\) and every set O of output strings, \(\Pr [M(D)\in O]\le e\cdot \Pr [M(D' )\in O]+1/(100n^{2})\). M uses independent fair random bits and has one worst-case polynomial bound \(p(n+d)\) on bit operations, output length and random bits. Its output is a finite binary string S. E receives d,S,J,a, has a worst-case bound given by one polynomial in d+|S| and outputs a binary-encoded rational number. E has no access to D, private state of M or an additional oracle. Both algorithms are ordinary classical Turing machines, with no nonuniform advice. The accuracy event is simultaneous over all queries and its probability is over M’s randomness alone, separately for every D. S need not encode a synthetic database or a consistent probability distribution. \(C,\alpha ,p,M,E\) and the evaluator’s polynomial are fixed before d,D are chosen. No algorithm to compute \(\alpha\) and no prescribed rate of its convergence are required.
answer_criterion: Prove the proposition in the problem statement or its logical negation, with all definitions, promises, resource bounds and quantifiers as stated. A conditional result establishes only the explicitly conditional claim. Benchmark acceptance requires a complete proof-assistant-verified proof of the full target.
why: Determine whether the information-theoretic usefulness of private high-dimensional statistics can be achieved with polynomial computation and polynomially many records.

importance.reason: A fundamental statistical-versus-computational gap for a concrete and widely used query family. It complements existing sample-complexity questions and has an explicit specialist open-problem formulation, while allowing non-synthetic outputs avoids a known source of misleading hardness claims.

progress.text: Private marginal release on small databases is achieved with subexponential per-query computation and fixed additive error.

context_blocks.text: A marginal measures the fraction of records matching a pattern on selected coordinates. Low-order marginals describe small groups of attributes, while all marginals permit every such pattern. The family contains exponentially many queries even though one query has a short description. A synopsis is therefore an efficiently evaluable representation, rather than a literal list of exponentially many answers.

Privacy and accuracy quantify different objects. The privacy guarantee compares the complete output distributions after changing one person’s row. Accuracy concerns all queries simultaneously on each fixed database. Once a successful synopsis has been released, its deterministic evaluation reveals no additional access to the original records. An algorithm answering only a prespecified small batch is not automatically an algorithm for this target.

Vadhan’s Open Problem 7.8 asks about polynomial-time private estimation of all higher-order marginals with vanishing error using only polynomially many rows in the dimension. The present card fixes approximate-DP parameters, replacement adjacency and a noninteractive evaluable synopsis. These choices state one concrete version of the proposal; they are not asserted to be equivalent to every interactive or fixed-order formulation.

Chandrasekaran, Thaler, Ullman and Wan give subexponential-time private algorithms for marginal queries on small databases. Their result illustrates useful progress between exponential and polynomial cost. The constant-accuracy, per-query statement in that paper does not provide the polynomial-time, vanishing-error synopsis required here.

Requiring synthetic records would impose an extra restriction. The benchmark permits any binary synopsis with an efficient evaluator, because hardness of synthetic-data generation need not rule out other ways of answering queries. The existing TCS-0506 concerns private PAC sample complexity, while TCS-6040 asks about strong approximation of coverage functions. Neither asks this computational query-release question.
